ASRSN:2241569.n: Was assigned 2000' after takeoff, after takeoff the auto pilot was engaged at approx.500' agl and the electric trim ran away, after disengaging the auto pilot and pitching down we had already reached an altitude of 2300 but quickly returned to 2000 as we were informed there was traffic very close Was advised to call atc and did so explaining the issue we had. Will be discussing with Textron as we have had several software issues with this aircraft.On the next flight the autopilot was engaged and turned the aircraft in the opposite direction that it was commanded, this did not happen in any airspace that was critical.
ASRSN:2241569.s: The pilot reported autopilot trim runaway and incorrect turn commands on a Textron aircraft shortly after takeoff. These software issues caused an altitude deviation to 2300 feet and required manual correction to avoid nearby traffic.

ASRSN:2241576.n: Night VFR flight with a CFI from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2, though I was acting as PIC. Low oil pressure approximately 70 miles west of ZZZ. Oil annunciator light was flickering, and then I noticed the oil pressure gauge was reading in the yellow arc lower than normal. Tried to troubleshoot the problem by reference to the POH, and alerted ATC of the problem. The oil annunciator light then went from flickering to a steady glow, which I then advised ZZZ center on XXX.XX. A corrective action was taken to divert to ZZZ3, and overfly the Interstate in the event that I suffered an engine failure I would have a set place to land. ZZZ center informed me that ZZZ3's runway was closed per NOTAM and ZZZ4 was the next closest option. I then requested priority handling with Albuquerque center. I was handed off to ZZZ1 approach where I was given a bravo [airspace] clearance after I requested to overfly ZZZ4 at 9500 feet and circle down in the event the engine failed. I had a normal, uneventful landing. Oil pressure was at zero by the time I landed.
ASRSN:2241576.s: The pilot of a CFI-conducted night VFR flight experienced low oil pressure and a flickering annunciator light, prompting a diversion. After being advised the initial alternate was closed, the pilot received priority handling and a bravo clearance to overfly the next airport at 9500 feet before landing safely with zero oil pressure.

ASRSN:2241579.n: Date / Location / Time: On Day 0, at ZZZ around XA:00 I was landing Turbo Commander 840 on runway XX on a VFR flight. The conditions of the airport environment were dry, low wind with low traffic.Purpose: This purpose of this flight was to transport the aircraft, post maintenance. I was PIC and the only occupant of the aircraft. Preflight Factors: The aircraft owner had consistently reported and advised of a low horsepower issue, particularly noticeable during landing. However, this issue could not be replicated during multiple test flights conducted at Service Center in ZZZ1.Upon leaving the service center, the flaps were also noted inoperative due to an asymmetric deployment condition, resolving this would require a cable replacement. Conversation regarding no flaps flight in the aircraft with the Commander Service Center indicated a ferry flight would not be required. The aircraft was released from the service center maintenance on Day 0 and subsequently flown by me to ZZZ on the flight in issue on Day 0.First Landing at ZZZ on Runway XY: The horsepower on both engines, particularly the left engine, remained unusually high during the approach, with the left engine indicating between 200 and 230 HP. This residual power made it difficult to slow the aircraft, a challenge further compounded by the inability to deploy flaps for additional drag. As a result, touchdown occurred above blue line airspeed. This landing was otherwise normal and was to a full stop and taxi back to runway XY. Second Takeoff From Runway XY: A second takeoff was conducted to verify the potential engine power issues in a controlled manner. The goal was to accurately identify and document the abnormality to communicate this to maintenance staff ahead of scheduled owner training in the coming weeks.Lower Power: During the takeoff roll, engine and airspeed seemed to advance normally. However, at rotation, it appeared the aircraft engines were not producing the expected power output and acceleration. In the moment, I needed to make a timely decision whether to abort or continue the takeoff. All factors considered and remaining runway length, I opted to continue the takeoff. In an effort to assist with potential lower power, decided to retract the gear right at that moment, earlier than normal, to reduce drag and aid climbout.Event: However, due to the low energy state and normal motion of flight, the aircraft belly briefly contacted the runway on the belly before managing a climbout. The pattern flight continued without incident, and I landed normally back on runway XY.
ASRSN:2241579.s: The PIC of a Turbo Commander 840, operating with inoperative flaps and suspected low engine power, experienced a brief belly contact during a second takeoff at ZZZ. The pilot attributed the incident to insufficient acceleration and an early gear retraction attempt to aid climbout.

ASRSN:2241580.n: Flying on course from the YONMA Fix direct OMMNI Waypoint, about 3.6 miles southwest of the PUNQU Waypoint, I encountered a hang glider at my 12 o'clock opposite direction at the same altitude. I advised ATC that I would be making a turn and climb to avoid him. Prior to commencing a turn and climb, I saw an additional hang glider about 150 ft at my 10 o'clock at 4,000 ft (now 100 ft below). Looking back to my now 3 o'clock on a 310 heading and about 200 ft at 4,000 (still 100 ft below) popping out of a cloud. At this time, there are now three (3) hang gliders all at 4,000 flying into and out of clouds. Within 3 minutes of seeing and taking evasive maneuvers, I advised ATC that I was clear of conflict and continued back on course.The weather conditions in the area of the incident were SCT 4000 ft with the clouds being cumulus clouds with tops of about 4500-5000 ft. In the location, the clouds were roughly 200 ft to the North and 100 ft to the West.No conflict alert was given by ATC due to the hang gliders not appearing on RADAR.No other issues were encountered for the remainder of the flight.
ASRSN:2241580.s: The pilot encountered three hang gliders at 4,000 feet while flying from YONMA to OMMNI in scattered clouds. The pilot executed a turn and climb to avoid the non-radar targets, which were popping in and out of clouds, and reported clear of conflict three minutes later.

ASRSN:2241586.n: 1. What happened?While flying my drone (UAS) for a commercial mapping mission on Day 0, I inadvertently launched in Class D airspace near ZZZ. I did not have a LAANC authorization at the time of the flight. I became aware of the violation after the flight when I checked my airspace map/app more carefully and realized the location was within an actively controlled airspace boundary.2. Why did it happen?This occurred due to human factors on my part when planning a multi-site mission. I had previously reviewed the area using Aloft, but I had mistakenly confused this site with a separate site that was just outside of the ZZZ Class D Airspace. It was not my intention to violate any FAA rules, and I was unaware of the airspace classification at the time of launch.3. What actions did you take?Once I realized the airspace violation at the next site which I had confused the airspace with, I immediately researched the previous flight area and mission. Upon realizing my failure, I informed myself on the necessary means to self-report, along with a performing post-incident review of my actions and the preceding conditions. I am now filing this report in an effort to take full responsibility and contribute to overall safety awareness.4. What could have prevented this?A more thorough pre-flight planning system and check list would have prevented this incident. This was an error of organization and pre-flight double checking.5. What will you do differently in the future?I am implementing a system to identify and write down site-specific issues for flight missions prior to flight. In addition, I am committing to complete my pre-flight checklist that includes confirming airspace with FAA-authorized LAANC apps and reviewing airspace class boundaries before each flight. I also intend to keep updated on UAS regulations regularly.
ASRSN:2241586.s: A commercial drone operator inadvertently launched a UAS in Class D airspace near ZZZ without LAANC authorization due to confusing the site with one outside the controlled boundary. The operator self-reported the violation after realizing the error and plans to implement stricter pre-flight checklists to prevent recurrence.

ASRSN:2241587.n: Was flying on Day 0, was late for my son's football games and didn't think to request authorization for flight space. I used my drone to record the games no higher than 30' off the ground and noticed multiple planes in the area. When I returned home that night I checked where I was flying and noticed it was right [next] to the Mesa airport with a 0' flight ceiling.
ASRSN:2241587.s: A drone operator flew a drone up to 30 feet near Mesa Airport without authorization while recording a football game. The operator later discovered the location had a zero-foot flight ceiling and noted multiple aircraft were present in the area.

ASRSN:2241598.n: Aircraft X was a maintenance reposition aircraft. I was training someone at the time. The trainee issued '1, 2' to enter their ramp. Aircraft X then decided to take [taxiway] 3 and turned right on 4, which is opposite direction to the traffic flow. There was Aircraft Y coming down 4 on the opposite direction that slammed on their brakes. When I told Aircraft X to stop, they said the ramp told them to do it. This is a recurring problem that this airline does all the time. We have an MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) with the Terminal X ramp control that explicitly states that the ramp cannot tell aircraft to reverse direction on a taxiway. It's also a movement area, which they do not have control over. Share this with the airline. This happens all the time and is not ok. Someone is going to get hurt one of these days from slamming on the brakes.
ASRSN:2241598.s: An air traffic controller reported that a maintenance reposition aircraft, directed by ramp control to reverse direction on a taxiway, caused an opposing aircraft to slam on its brakes. The controller stated this violated the Terminal X MOU and movement area rules, creating a recurring safety risk.

ASRSN:2241599.n: Fighters calling for taxi for departure to XXR one after the other. Aircraft X followed by Aircraft Z followed by Aircraft A and Aircraft B. Aircraft Y was on a visual approach to RWY XYR about 5 mi final Aircraft X in position for departure on XXR. I looked at the fighter strips as they taxied out to note the number in flight. It appeared that Aircraft X was a flight of 2, however, they we actually a flight of 4 and the way it was written kind of looked like a 2 with a slant. I cleared the fighters for take-off and switched to departure then I noticed more fighters to start to roll after the first 2 then I questioned how many were in the flight. Upon closer inspection it was a flight of 4. At this point Aircraft Y was over XXR and did not over fly any of the aircraft departing but it did split the flight. I'm unsure if the 3rd or 4th fighter delayed their departure because they observed the traffic.One possible solution is to verify the number in flight either by the fighters telling us on check in when they call for taxi or having the LC (Local Control) controller verifying.
ASRSN:2241599.s: An air traffic controller cleared a flight of four fighters for departure from RWY XXR after misreading the strip as two aircraft. An arriving aircraft split the departing formation, and the controller noted the third and fourth fighters may have delayed takeoff due to the traffic.

ASRSN:2241602.n: We checked on with ZZZ approach and were assigned the visual approach to XXR. We were given vectors for the right downwind and later told to expect the visual to XXL. We were given vectors to join the localizer and advised of corporate aircraft (Aircraft Y) traffic at our 3 o'clock. I had the aircraft in sight, it appeared it had been following us on the same left downwind. We were told to maintain visual separation with the corporate traffic, maintain 160 knots to the bridge, and cleared for the visual to runway XXL. I had the traffic in sight for the entire base and final legs. Our approach speed was around 156knots due to the wind, so we were not going to have to slow down too much after the bridge. We appeared to be gaining on Aircraft Y and we subsequently got a TA. After 20 seconds or so, we received a 'DESCEND, DESCEND' RA at approximately 1,300 ft. I smoothly complied with the RA (the automation was already off). The CA reported the TCAS RA to the tower. At around 700 feet we simultaneously got a 'MONITOR VERTICAL SPEED' RA and a 'Glide slope' EGPWS warning. I arrested the descent, added power and flew just below the red box which resulted in a slight climb. Shortly thereafter, we received the 'CLEAR OF CONFLICT' advisory. During the procedure, I lost visual contact with the aircraft. We executed a normal go around and conducted an uneventful visual approach and landing to XXL after.
ASRSN:2241602.s: The flight crew received a TCAS RA and EGPWS warning while on a visual approach to runway XXL due to gaining on a corporate aircraft. They executed a go-around after complying with the RA and arresting the descent, then landed uneventfully on a subsequent approach.

ASRSN:2241616.n: Original departure time was delayed 1.5 hours. During takeoff roll left Eng failed to produce t/o power and t/o was rejected at 80kts. Accomplished checklist items and consulted Maintenance Control/return to gate took 30 minutes. Tail swap was going to be required which would take atleast another hour. The flight was a ZZZ turn planned landing time of XA00. With the high stress event occurring and now having an estimated land time of XD:00 with little opportunity for rest since the planned break period being 30-45min we determined it was unsafe to continue trip at current fatigue level.
ASRSN:2241616.s: The crew rejected takeoff at 80 knots due to left engine failure, requiring a tail swap that caused significant delays. Facing reduced rest time and high stress, the crew determined it was unsafe to continue the trip due to fatigue.

ASRSN:2241618.n: When I called Flap 5 after start checklist, FO moved Flap handle. When flaps moved to 5 we both heard a shimmy from the control handle. I called for 15 to check, shimmy was worse. We set 5, shimmy was present. We called Maintenance Control. Returned to gate. At Gate, Gate Agent wanted us to remain on aircraft for maint to troubleshoot. I met Maint on the Jet Bridge to explain situation. They disclosed (we also know) previous flight reported Severe Turbulence. I worked with maint after passengers deplaned to replicate the shimmy. It returned much worse and louder when flaps set to 20. Shortly afterward, I believe cable control snapped. We lost complete control of flap position - handle moved, but flaps did not. Maint said we were lucky and maybe something was missed on previous post flight inspection.
ASRSN:2241618.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced a worsening flap handle shimmy during pre-flight checks, which led to a return to the gate. The reporter believes a cable snapped after replicating the issue with flaps at 20, causing a total loss of flap control, possibly due to missed maintenance following previous severe turbulence.

ASRSN:2241638.n: When setting takeoff power noticed excessive EGT split between the left and right engines. The split was in excess of 250 degrees. Rejected the takeoff around 90 knots. Ran appropriate checklists and returned to the ramp. We taxied out to Runway XX at ZZZ. We were issued a clearance and an initial heading on departure. The captain taxied the aircraft onto the runway and transferred the controls to me. I initiated the takeoff and called for autothrottles and 'check thrust'. A few seconds later, the captain called reject and took control of the aircraft. He later stated that he had noticed a large split between the engine EGTs and said that there could have been more going on, but he noticed the EGTs and decided to reject at a lower speed, rather than continue into the high speed regime trying to diagnose the issue. I looked down at the speed tape and we were just slightly above 80kts. I let the tower know that we were rejecting, and we exited runway XX at taxiway 1 to allow a CRJ on final to land. Once clear of the runway, we completed the 'Rejected Takeoff QRC' and the associated checklist in the flight manual. Using the cooling table and monitoring the brake temps, we determined that it was safe to return to the ramp. We taxied to the ramp and shutdown the aircraft without further incident.
ASRSN:2241638.s: The First Officer initiated takeoff but the Captain rejected it at approximately 80 knots due to an excessive 250-degree EGT split between engines. The crew safely exited the runway, completed checklists, and returned to the ramp without incident.

ASRSN:2241653.n: At the Gate:During ZZZ preflight, the flight deck oxygen was shut off for about 45 minutes. So, we called and were told this was due to O2 servicing as part of the ETOPS service check. What we did not know -- and could not see due to it being a maintenance-initiated action -- was that the inbound O2 pressure had been discovered to be zero following the flight from ZZZZ. That crew must not have gotten the EICAS, or it happened after they left the aircraft. Either way, maintenance elected to change an O2 bottle. Before we closed the door, I requested the maintenance tech come to the flight deck to ensure our masks were working correctly. He did so, and the oxygen level was checked to be 1700 psi. All four oxygen masks were tested, and all mask-door positions were checked before departure. They were left alone after that. The tech did not explain the extent of the maintenance performed or any issues encountered due to that maintenance.About 20 minutes later, we finally got the release and departed late. I reviewed the current release only and did not dig into the new maintenance history as I had no indication that anything other than servicing" had occurred. (See maintenance part of resolution narrative later in this report.)During cruise:About 5 hours into the flight to ZZZZ1, we got an EICAS, "CREW OXYGEN LOW." The checklist was very short and confirmed the situation. After completing the checklist, our O2 pressure indicated about 800 psi. But, when we checked our masks, the flight deck oxygen pressure went to zero, and all four masks went flat -- NO oxygen available! We immediately brought four walk-around 02 bottles to the flight deck to ensure a source of oxygen in the event of depressurization. We then called Maintenance Control and Dispatch and patched in the Chief Pilot. All agreed that we could NOT continue to ZZZZ1 because operation with just walk-around bottles did not meet safety standards in the event of fire and/or smoke. So, we decided our best option was to turn back to ZZZ1. The diversion and overweight checklists were both run. FOM X.XX.X was reviewed. With Maintenance Control and Dispatch input, and due to the high approach speeds for overweight and flaps 25 versus 30, we elected to jettison about 25,000 pounds of fuel at FL270 to facilitate landing at maximum landing weight.The diversion and landing just under MLW in ZZZ1 were both uneventful. Per the FOM diversion recovery guide, the crew stayed with the aircraft until passengers were deplaned, and the aircraft was turned over to ZZZ1 Maintenance.The value of communication was evident during this event. The divert itself was coordinated via a "urgent" message through CPDLC. This was interpreted as having [requested priority handling], though we had not. The only emergency authority used was to dump the fuel."
ASRSN:2241653.s: The flight crew diverted to ZZZ1 during cruise after a "CREW OXYGEN LOW" EICAS indicated zero pressure, caused by an uncommunicated maintenance bottle change at the gate. The crew jettisoned 25,000 pounds of fuel at FL270 to land under maximum landing weight, as walk-around bottles did not meet safety standards for the original destination.

ASRSN:2241664.n: On the descent into SFO around FL290 we hit what we thought was severe turbulence. After the initial bump I made the 'flight attendants be seated immediately' PA. The event lasted approximately 15 seconds and the passenger seat belt sign was on at the time of the occurrence. After the event ended I made the 'flight attendants take your jumpseat' PA.After reporting the event to ATC we were informed that we were in trail of a heavy 777 and because it was a brief and isolated event we assumed that it was wake turbulence.Nobody was injured and an ELB (Electronic Log Book) was submitted
ASRSN:2241664.s: During descent into SFO at FL290, the crew encountered severe turbulence lasting 15 seconds while the seat belt sign was on. The event was attributed to wake turbulence from a trailing heavy 777, resulting in no injuries and an ELB submission.

ASRSN:2241669.n: We planned and were cleared for a visual approach Rwy XX , which we briefed would be backed up with the RNAV (RNP) Y XX approach. The FMGC was properly programmed and GPS remained HIGH for the entire approach on the PROG page. We had our brick, stick, and two FMAs as the approach was being conducted in final app. We were cleared for the visual approach and joined. the inbound course just outside of ZZZZZ (6.5 miles from the runway) and descended to 2000. The vertical deviation showed us high the entire time as we began the descent We descended to catch the electronic GPS glide slope and the first officer disconnected the autopilot. Just outside of ZZZZZ1 at 1300', we were still getting a full fly down indication on our vertical glide slope showing we were high we both noted all 4 PAPI's for XX were red. At that point in instructed the first officer to ignore the GPS glide slope and follow the PAPI's. I also based this off of distance to the runway and our altitude. An uneventful landing ensued.
ASRSN:2241669.s: The flight crew conducted a visual approach to Runway XX, noting a discrepancy between the GPS glide slope indicating high and the red PAPI lights. The captain instructed the first officer to ignore the GPS deviation and follow the PAPIs, resulting in an uneventful landing.

ASRSN:2241670.n: In light of the issues with EWR and the TRACON losing comms and radar capability, I'm wondering if there can be some coordination between companies and the FAA at either the national level or the local level. As I write this, there have been no fewer than 3 known equipment failures in the EWR approach area in the last week to 10 days. I took the time to review lost communication procedures, and I noticed one major flaw: there is no timeline given for determining when one is to be considered in a NORDO situation. This leaves every pilot/plane/flight/crew to their own devices when it comes to determining when 'lost comm' has occurred. What is considered an appropriate time? 1 minute? 90 seconds? 5 minutes? Any of these times can be considered an eternity at 250 knots below 10,000 or when over 250 above 10. Like any pilot, I've had gaps due to controller shift changes, controllers working multiple frequencies, or dead zones near an antenna. But the reality is that the AIM (Aeronautical Information Manual) gives little to no help in determining how long we should wait before initiating lost comm procedures. Is there any way to work with the FAA to craft an agreement on when it is considered an appropriate time to initiate lost comm procedures, especially into EWR and the NYC area? Leaving every flight to work 'by guess and by golly' does not sound like a reasonable business plan, and some common template would be helpful.
ASRSN:2241670.s: A pilot reported multiple recent equipment failures causing communication and radar loss in the EWR approach area. The reporter identified a lack of specific timelines in the AIM for initiating lost communication procedures, creating uncertainty for crews operating at various speeds and altitudes.

ASRSN:2241691.n: When loading the aircraft, I grabbed a case. For some reason or another the case wasn't properly latched and camera supplies spilled over the Ramp. Among the supplies many Li ion batteries were found in the supplies. Including a few camera spare batteries and a large power bank. I let my team lead know who called a supervisor.Apparently, the passenger had another case and gate check which the Ramp crew pulled from the flight, and apparently (hearsay) he has traveled on multiple flight with Li ion batteries in checked luggage.
ASRSN:2241691.s: Ramp crew discovered spilled Li-ion batteries from an unlatched passenger case during aircraft loading. The supervisor was notified, and the passenger reportedly had a second checked bag containing batteries and a history of traveling with them in checked luggage.

ASRSN:2241706.n: Type of event: Hoverboard (Voltage:36V with Capacity:20Ah, Built in Rechargeable Lithium-ion battery) found in the customer's checked in bag. Location: ZZZZ. Description: ZZZZ transfer bag security screener took it out from the bag, handed it over to us. It will be disposed according to ZZZZ Airport hazard disposal procedure.
ASRSN:2241706.s: A security screener at ZZZZ Airport discovered a 36V lithium-ion hoverboard in a passenger's checked bag during transfer screening. The item was removed and will be disposed of according to airport hazard procedures.

ASRSN:2241731.n: Passenger arrived at ZZZ for flight to ZZZ1. Pax had a 230lb, 158 inch motorized/electric tricycle. According to Company policyCompany does not accept recreational battery powered motor devices. However management allowed passenger to check in the item with theStipulation that pax can not bring on board the lithium battery that operates this devise. Contacted Company dangerous goods Who advised pax can not bring on board the aircraft the lithium battery, and pax may have had two lithium batteries. It is a meet one e-trike with 750 w rear motor
ASRSN:2241731.s: A passenger attempted to check a 230lb, 750W motorized tricycle with lithium batteries at ZZZ, violating company policy against recreational battery devices. Management allowed the item only after the passenger agreed to remove the batteries, though Dangerous Goods advised the passenger might have possessed two batteries.

ASRSN:2241753.n: On final approach after selecting gear down, we received a HYD SYS 1 failure, with associated amber and cyan messages on the EICAS, approximately 5 seconds after gear extension. We confirmed that the landing gear was down and locked, and all indications were normal.Referencing the QRH, we noted that landing performance would be affected, requiring an increase in landing distance by a factor of 1.6. Based on our weight and runway available, we determined that we could safely land and elected to continue the approach.After a normal touchdown, we were unable to taxi due to loss of nosewheel steering, so we came to a stop on the runway and advised ATC of the issue. We completed the After Landing Checklist and reviewed the Hydraulic System 1 failure procedures in the QRH. ATC [gave us priority handling] on our behalf. The landing itself was uneventful and all systems remained stable post-landing.The Captain coordinated with Maintenance and Dispatch, while I was delegated to communicate with ATC and update the passengers. Ground personnel advised that the aircraft could not be towed with passengers onboard, so we arranged for a shuttle bus and deplaned passengers on the runway.The airplane was towed to a parking spot. After the aircraft was parked, it was noted that there was a broken hydraulic line.
ASRSN:2241753.s: The crew experienced a Hydraulic System 1 failure on final approach, requiring a 1.6 landing distance increase but allowing a safe touchdown. Post-landing, loss of nosewheel steering prevented taxiing, leading to a runway deplaning and discovery of a broken hydraulic line.

ASRSN:2241763.n: After liftoff at gear up master caution, engine 1 hydraulic low pressure and electric hydraulic pump #2 low pressure lights illuminated. Ran hydraulic low pressure checklist. Both hydraulic system pressures were normal, but the engine 1 hydraulic low pressure light remained illuminated before and after turning off engine 1 hydraulic pump switch. Climbed to safe altitude and received vectors to land XXC. [Requested priority handling] for overweight landing. Landed successfully and returned to gate. Cause: Hydraulic system failure. Immediately after rotation and during landing gear retraction we received a master caution with a Hyd low pressure on the engine 1 side. Both engine 1 hyd pump and electric pump 2 showed low pressure. CA ran hydraulic low pressure checklist and we continued to climb to a safe altitude while we decided to return to ZZZ. [Requested priority handling] and returned for an overweight landing about 20 min later. Cause: Hydraulic system failure.
ASRSN:2241763.s: The flight crew experienced a hydraulic system failure on Engine 1 immediately after liftoff, triggering low pressure warnings for both the engine and electric pumps. They executed the checklist, climbed to a safe altitude, and returned for a successful overweight landing with priority handling.

ASRSN:2241773.n: The CA was the PM and the FO was the PF for flight ABCD ZZZ to ZZZ1During cruise flight at 31,000 we got an AIR PACK 1 and 2 FAULT ECAM (PACK 2 and BLEED 2 was already on MEL XX-XXX). We applied non normal methodology as per training. The PF started an immediate descent and the PM checked QRC and stared ECAM procedures. Due to the ECAM procedures we saw that the cabin altitude was increasing and changed the immediate descent to an emergency descent. As the cabin altitude reached 9500 feet we got the CAB PR EXCESS CAB ALT. We reapplied non normal methodology and completed the QRC and ECAM procedures while performing an emergency descent to 10,000 feet. Once the aircraft was stabilized at 10,000 feet the I called the flight attendants to advise them the oxygen was no longer needed and made a detailed announcement to the passengers explaining what had happened and that we had applied procedures to keep the aircraft safe and were going make a precautionary landing at ZZZ2. With the aircraft now stabilized at a safe altitude we reviewed the situation and our actions and confirmed that diverting to ZZZ2 was the best course of action considering weather (clear VFR), passenger service and aircraft maintenance. After confirming that the company was informed of our diversion we made a visual approach to runway XXC. After exiting the runway, ZZZ2 CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) followed us to gate XX where the passengers deplaned to the terminal. What I would have done better and was able to take away from the situation:The good: preplaning and identifying a single pack operation as a threat preflight and staying at a lower altitude with extra fuel, both on the way out to ZZZ and the incident flight back to ZZZ1, allowed us to get down quicker than flying at the field FL370 (to ZZZ1) and FL360 (to ZZZ). Several Take aways items when I review the incident post flight as I write this:Should I experience a situation like this again, meaning anything to do with pressurization, I will immediately start an emergency descent, I was surprised how fast the cabin climbed.I contacted the flight attendants with a call when I should have made the PA, Emergency Descent, Be Seated". How hard it is to communicate with the oxygen masks on. Also mask O2 setting are difficult to set when you are used to seeing the front of the mask during an O2 test while setting up the cockpit versus when the O2 mask is donned. While I feel I did a good job communicating with the passengers during the incident and while enroute to ZZZ2 I didn't realize how much the cabin would warm up due to the O2 generators and Pack situation. The FAs (Flight Attendants) commented to me how warm the cabin was when we were enroute to ZZZ2. Had realized this, I would have included it in my PA to the passengers when below 10,000 feet explaining to them what had happened, that the aircraft was in a safe condition and we were going to land in ZZZ2. I would have told them the cabin may feel warmer due to the heat from the O2 generators." We were issued an aircraft with #2 PACK/Bleed on MEL. We had flown the aircraft from ZZZ1 to ZZZ without issue. On the return flight to ZZZ1 at FL310 we received the AIR PACK 1 FAULT ECAM. This immediately transitioned into PACK 1+2 FAULT that required an immediate descent to FL100. We were monitoring the cabin pressure altitude on the EICAS page and it held for a short time and then started to rapidly increase. We donned our oxygen masks, [requested priority handling] with ATC and advised them of the situation and that we were continuing our descent to FL100. We accomplished the ECAM procedures and follow up procedures and made the decision to divert to ZZZ2. We were 100 miles from ZZZ2 so we continued the descent to FL050 to help stabilize the pressurization better and proceeded direct the airfield. We had a normal approach and landing and taxied to the gate without issues for a normal deplaning.Cause: Issuing an aircraft with a single PACK. Dispatcher had us filed for the max operating altitude for a single PACK, we elected to fly lower, which ultimately saved us over a minute in the descent and breathing on supplemental O2.
ASRSN:2241773.s: The flight crew of flight ABCD experienced a dual air pack failure at FL310 while operating with Pack 2 on MEL, causing rapid cabin altitude increase and requiring an emergency descent to 10,000 feet. The crew diverted to ZZZ2 for a precautionary landing, attributing the incident to dispatching an aircraft with a single pack at maximum operating altitude.

ASRSN:2241776.n: During the takeoff roll on Runway 23L from MMMX, at a point after 80 knots, we passed over a very significant bump on the runway surface. The bump was so substantial it caused the premature and uncommanded rotation of the aircraft as the nose gear passed over it. I had to fly the nose gear back down to the runway to continue our acceleration to Vr speed. I consider this to be a significant hazard and must be addressed by the airport.Fix the runway.
ASRSN:2241776.s: The pilot reported that during the takeoff roll on Runway 23L at MMMX, a significant runway bump caused uncommanded rotation after 80 knots. The pilot manually lowered the nose gear to continue acceleration, identifying the surface defect as a hazard requiring airport repair.

ASRSN:2241782.n: Loaded Li Batteries forward baggage above fire line. Cause: Rush to close on time
ASRSN:2241782.s: Crew loaded lithium batteries in forward baggage above the fire line due to a rush to close on time.

ASRSN:2241816.n: On climb out we got HYD 2 LOW QTY EICAS message and immediately referenced the QRH. We noticed HYD 2 was amber and continued to monitor it deepen into the amber. We messaged dispatch via ACARS and informed them we would like maintenance [upon] arrival. Shortly after the electric pump turned on followed by the HYD SYS 2 FAIL. Autopilot kicked off and captain took the aircraft and radios. We [requested priority handling] and started on the HYD SYS 2 FAIL QRH. We messaged dispatch and advised our FA (Flight Attenddant] and received priority handing to Runway XXC from ATC. We shot the RNAV and broke out around 2200. We exited the runway and cancelled the priority handling. Maintenance met us at the gate.
ASRSN:2241816.s: During climb out, the crew received HYD 2 LOW QTY and HYD SYS 2 FAIL messages, causing autopilot disengagement. The captain manually flew the aircraft, received priority handling from ATC, and landed safely for maintenance inspection.

ASRSN:2241921.n: A check vavle in hydraulic nose compartment on a t fitting was installed incorrectly causing system 1 accumulator to not receive hydraulic fluid. And not allowing the landing gear to be retractable.Suggestion: Triple check work prior to doing sign off.
ASRSN:2241921.s: A mechanic incorrectly installed a check valve in the hydraulic nose compartment, preventing System 1 accumulator from receiving fluid and rendering the landing gear non-retractable. The reporter attributed the issue to improper installation and suggested triple-checking work before sign-off.

ASRSN:2241928.n: All of the DG-1000 sailplanes do not have spoiler position labels on the rear seat pilot position. As a result, the spoiler could be a percent open on landing without the rear seat pilot or instructor being aware of its position. Also, on takeoff the rear seat pilot often cannot determine that the spoilers are locked.Event happened to me when an instructor in the rear seat took over controls while landing at 20 feet altitude. I was in the front seat and had spoilers 3/4 deployed. I released the controls to the instructor as he requested HIS AIRCRAFT. Problem, at 10 feet the instructor pulled the spoiler, but they were already open. As a result, the sailplane contacted the runway at a heavy contact on the main wheel but then nosed over as the brake was activated at that spoiler position. The sailplane then swerved sideways because we're just a few degrees not straight, and the sailplane ground looped and slid sideways down the runway and came to a stop without any damage. Lucky. Had the rear seat pilot been aware of the spoiler position by the means of marking or placards the event may not have occurred.Suggest all DG-1000 sailplanes have markings or placards that indicate the position of the spoiler control lever.
ASRSN:2241928.s: A front-seat pilot and rear-seat instructor in a DG-1000 sailplane experienced a heavy landing and ground loop at 10 feet because the instructor unknowingly pulled already deployed spoilers. The reporter attributes the incident to missing spoiler position labels at the rear seat, which prevented awareness of the control lever's status.

ASRSN:2241929.n: The purpose of flight was to train employees in using Unmanned aircraft to identify mosquito habitat to assist in eradication.I was training employees of County Public Health on Basic UAS flying with my DJI Phantom 4 pro. The area flown was at Location A. I obtained a standard weather brief over the phone with FSS and and an authorization of 50 feet AGL using the LAANC system through ALOFT. I gave a preflight briefing to the employees especially emphasizing the 50 foot altitude restrictions. We performed some basic maneuvers in the morning session. Then in the second session after XA00 a few of the students exceeded 50 feet AGL I think the maximum was 86 feet and I took the controls back and corrected, It seemed some were confusing left stick vs right stick and we were practicing using the telemetry to orientate the drone back towards the home point when disoriented. VLOS was maintained while we practiced this. Furthermore I was having trouble setting maximum altitude on the drone. Whenever I tried to set it for 15 meters, the software kept resetting to 45 meters. after several attempts with no success to reset, I advised the employees to use the telemetry to monitor their altitude. At postflight, after XD00 pm, we discussed that we should use a different facility within at least a two hundred grid to practice in and set maximum altitude to 100 feet to insure a safe buffer.
ASRSN:2241929.s: A UAS instructor training County Public Health employees on a DJI Phantom 4 Pro at Location A reported students exceeding the authorized 50-foot AGL limit due to control confusion and software altitude reset issues. The instructor regained control, maintained VLOS, and recommended using a different facility with a higher altitude buffer for future training.

ASRSN:2241937.n: On Day 0, I was conducting a biannual flight review for Person A in his aircraft, a Mooney M20F. I completed his ground training the previous day over a video conference before the flight in accordance with 14 CFR 61.56, and we had agreed to complete the flight the following day due to conflicting schedules. We decided to meet at the airport for a XA:30 flight on the day of the flight so that we could be wheels up by no later than XB:00. The beginning of the flight was perfectly routine, and we departed ZZZ to the east to complete the required aerial work. Upon completing the aerial work, which Person A had failed to do, I instructed Person A to proceed back to ZZZ so we could complete the necessary landings and finish the required items for his flight review. Upon entering the traffic pattern for the first circuit, Person A demonstrated that he had an understanding and capability to land the aircraft successfully. We made a full stop taxi back to runway XX. I instructed Person A to demonstrate a short field takeoff and landing for the second circuit. Person A displayed some confusion about how to execute the maneuver, so I talked him through the proper execution of the maneuver before entering the runway environment. During the takeoff roll, Person A lacked understanding of what speed to pitch the aircraft for, even after discussing the speed on the ground. After repeated verbal cues to correct the airspeed, Person A failed to do so, which resulted in me having to take positive control of the aircraft to prevent an accelerated stall approximately 300 feet AGL. Once we were safely established in the traffic pattern, I gave control of the plane back to Person A to complete the short field landing. Person A became confused about the difference between a red and green light displayed on the top left corner of the dashboard, I inquired if everything was alright because I could not see which light he was talking about. He told me everything was okay and would perform the landing as requested. He verbalized the before-landing checklist by calling out the required steps. However, he was fixated on the runway itself and failed to check the approach to final for additional traffic, which forced me to take my eyes out of the cockpit and verify no additional traffic. Instead of using a standard traffic pattern, he made a short approach with no dedicated base and final approach segments. When I could fully evaluate the situation and configuration of the aircraft, it was too late for me to grab the controls and execute a go-around. We proceeded to slide to a stop on runway XX. We evacuated the aircraft successfully without injuries to either me or Person A. Rescue services were dispatched to remove the plane from runway XX.As for what I believe are contributing factors to this incident, Person A stated that he had not received any training in his aircraft since his last biannual several years ago, and that he needed this sign-off so that he could complete the upcoming flights, Person A stated he was not used to demonstrating the required maneuvers or procedures. After further questioning, Person A noted that a friend of his conducted his previous flight review and that this flight review was more strenuous than previous reviews. I believe a fixation on getting the sign-off resulted in a failure to recognize the aircraft's configuration. Resulting in a belly landing. As for me, the instructor, I believe my failure to recognize the aircraft configuration came from being distracted by having to clear the base and final approach. Transitioning back to the cockpit quickly resulted in my inability to recognize the landing gear in the up position. Resulting in a belly landing. As for corrective actions, I have already signed up for remedial training in the execution and instruction of complex aircraft, with an emphasis on identifying potential hazards and distractions that could lead to hazardous situations. Additionally, it should be emphasized that training is not simply a one-time occurrence every two years, we should all strive to be the best aviators we can be by developing a training regimen with a local flight club or school to maintain critical skills.
ASRSN:2241937.s: During a flight review in a Mooney M20F, the instructor and student executed a short-field landing with the gear up, resulting in a belly landing on runway XX. The incident was caused by the student's fixation on the runway and the instructor's distraction while clearing traffic, preventing recognition of the aircraft configuration.

ASRSN:2241947.n: I was waiting at the hold-short line for runway XX, and I heard another airplane self-announce that they were on base. They took a long time to turn final, and I thought their flying speed was pretty slow. I didn't see any traffic, so I thought I had enough space and time to take off. When I took off, the airplane that was trying to land said they were going around because I took the runway. As I took off, I saw the airplane on my right side and above.
ASRSN:2241947.s: The pilot held short of runway XX, observed a slow aircraft on base, and initiated takeoff believing the runway was clear. The landing aircraft executed a go-around after the pilot entered the runway, resulting in a close proximity encounter with the landing aircraft overhead.

ASRSN:2241955.n: I was cleared for takeoff on runway XX takeoff with a northeast left downwind departure and advise 'on the go'. A 172 took off in front of me. On climb out on departure leg I confirmed 'Left Downwind Departure' with the tower then I turned left crosswind shortly after the end of the runway.I did realize that the 172 was staying in the pattern as it seem to be far away, then I turned on a close downwind.On my downwind leg the tower pointed out the 172 which was on a parallel track to me in a wide downwind leg. I acknowledged the 172 as 'insight' to the tower and the 172 acknowledged me as 'insight' to the tower.Then as I was proceeding northeast bound I was advised of landing traffic at my 11 oclock, then advised 'hard right, do it now' to avoid landing traffic which I flew over with possibly 200 to 300 feet separation. The towers radar was offline. The command to turn hard right actually put me over of the path of landing traffic, the separation would have been better without the hard right command.Being a rotorcraft, I generally fly a tighter pattern if no others are in the pattern. My error was not realizing the 172 was staying in the pattern. If I had followed the 172, the timing would have been perfect, and this would have been a non-issue. With this incident it has become clear to me that my situational awareness of traffic in the pattern needs improvement.
ASRSN:2241955.s: A rotorcraft pilot departed behind a Cessna 172 but failed to realize the fixed-wing aircraft remained in the pattern. With radar offline, the pilot received a "hard right" avoidance command for landing traffic, resulting in 200–300 feet separation, which the pilot attributed to their own situational awareness error.

ASRSN:2241979.n: Landing at ZZZ, Runway XX. I operate from a dirt runway on my ranch, a private strip (ZZZ1). I do a carrier approach, very tight in. Been landing here for many years. The sequence is just backed in. On this day we landed using my usual procedure. We just came across Location A from ZZZ2 on an animal rescue mission. Very bumpy. Our cargo was a maine coon kitty coming from ZZZ3. Another pilot would finish the flight mission to final destination. I made my usual approach and inadvertently cut off students on 5 mile final. My bust, it wont happen again. Also I was accused of landing on the runway with another aircraft on the runway that had landed. I think he turned off mid field as I touched down on the numbers (short field mindset). By the time I got to the taxiway turn off, the other aircraft was already long gone. I don't really know if he had cleared before I touched down.
ASRSN:2241979.s: The pilot reported inadvertently cutting off student aircraft on final approach while landing a Maine Coon cat at a private dirt runway. The pilot also disputed an accusation of landing on an occupied runway, noting the other aircraft had likely cleared the field before touchdown.

ASRSN:2241985.n: After a clearance given through the D-side and flight data, Aircraft X departed. His clearance was to to ZZZ VOR climbing to 030. He turned 180 degrees left and got into terrain. We issued a low altitude alert and expedited his climb. When asking the pilot, he indicated he didn't know what 'cleared short to the VOR' meant. Not knowing exactly what was said over the phone with the pilot and FSS, I told him we'd sort it out, and later gave him the OM number to call. OJTI (On-the-job Training Instructor) in progress on the R-side, certified developmental on the D-side.RecommendationPilot needs to learn what 'cleared short' means. While working as the D-side on sector X I received a call from flight data with a ZZZ clearance request for Aircraft X. Clearance was issued clearing Aircraft X short to the ZZZ VOR. The routing on the initial read-back from flight data was incorrect and flight data had included the words as filed. I corrected flight data by stating that was incorrect and corrected them clarifying Aircraft X was cleared short to the ZZZ VOR. The second readback was correct and the call was finished. Upon departure Aircraft X started a 180-degree left turn away from the VOR and towards terrain. A low altitude alert was issued. The pilot seemed to have confusion regarding their clearance short to the VOR.RecommendationPilot needs clarification on clearance limit.
ASRSN:2241985.s: Aircraft X departed with a clearance short to ZZZ VOR but turned 180 degrees left into terrain due to the pilot's misunderstanding of the phrase. Air Traffic Control issued a low altitude alert and expedited the climb, noting the pilot required training on clearance limits.

ASRSN:2241987.n: Aircraft X on a vector over 3GM roughly 8NM South of MKG, while being vectored for the RNAV Runway 06, reported MKG in sight and requested the Visual Approach instead. I asked if there was a clear line of sight to the MKG airport as they were reporting a cloud layer lower than the aircraft. The pilot responded in the affirmative and was then cleared for the Visual Approach and told to contact MKG tower. I did NOT verify if the pilot had MKG vs 3GM because the aircraft was almost directly above 3GM. Very shortly after switching the aircraft to the tower, the Low Altitude Alert went off. I attempted multiple times to inform the tower of the alert. In the meantime, Aircraft X was observed making sharp turns and descents appearing to align with runway 09 at 3GM. On roughly the 4th attempt to contact MKG via the shout line, I informed the tower that it appeared that the aircraft was short final for the wrong airport/runway. The tower acknowledged. Upon seeing the aircraft appear to climb and then turn towards the north to MKG I attempted at least 2 more times to contact MKG and verify they had positive control of the aircraft to land on the correct runway. The wrong surface warning never activated, and the data block was current with the correct runway.Even though the aircraft was directly over the airport when the visual approach clearance was issued, I should have pointed out 3GM anyway. I didn't think the pilot would mistake the airports and runways. It's common practice to point out 3GM when it's visibly between the aircraft and the intended airport, but I didn't because he was directly over it.
ASRSN:2241987.s: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft X for a visual approach to MKG while the aircraft was over 3GM, failing to verify the pilot's airport identification. The pilot subsequently descended toward 3GM Runway 09, triggering a low altitude alert, before correcting course to MKG after the controller warned the tower.

ASRSN:2241989.n: At XA16Z Aircraft X C182 advised me of a request. When I responded, I wasn't able to reestablish comms with the aircraft and at XA19Z the aircraft's altitude reading was lost. I had another aircraft reach out and also asked Aircraft X IDENT if able. Then I observed the aircraft turn directly to ZZZ and subsequently issued the winds, altimeter, and location of ZZZ1 airport just in case, treating it as an emergency. I then observed the aircraft circle 1 mile west of ZZZ1 before radar contact was lost. I asked another VFR aircraft to circle the area and the local authorities were notified. The pilot called the controller in ZZZ tower saying their alternator malfunctioned and reported landing safely at ZZZ1 XA21Z.
ASRSN:2241989.s: Air Traffic Control lost communications and radar contact with a C182 due to an alternator malfunction. The controller treated the situation as an emergency, and the pilot subsequently landed safely at ZZZ1 airport.

ASRSN:2241992.n: Aircraft X was level at 050 SE bound. I handed him off to Center but failed to catch he was at 050 approaching a 060 MVA. Shortly after I switched Aircraft X to the receiving controller, I noticed the issue and promptly called Center and gave them control for his climb. At this point, I had been on position for over 2 hours, and was handling increased coordination, reference training on the Radar Assist position. I feel that in the future controllers should be on position less that 2 hours, especially when training is involved. While providing training on the Non control, Radar Assist position the Approach controller left an air craft level at 050 when entering an MVA of 060. Once I was made aware of the occurrence I endeavored to file a report. I would recommend all available positions be staffed during training, as the Approach controller was also working as CIC (Controller in Charge) during the time.
ASRSN:2241992.s: An Approach controller, who was also acting as Controller in Charge and training on the Radar Assist position, left Aircraft X level at 050 while approaching a 060 MVA. The controller later transferred the aircraft to Center for a climb after realizing the altitude conflict.

ASRSN:2241997.n: On approach to ZZZ, we received a TE FLAP ASYM EICAS message when extending the flaps from 15 to 20 while descending out of about 2500 feet, IAS of 180 and at or over ZZZZZ intersection for the RNAV XX. It was then confirmed by the flap position indicator indicating one flap position needle just past 15 and the other almost to 20. The landing gear was still retracted. We then advised the Tower Controller of our need to discontinue the approach and go around due to flap issue. We were given a 290 heading and initial climb to 2500 feet. Given our present altitude of about 2200 feet and cleared altitude of 2500 feet, we reset the MCP (Mode Control Panel) altitude window from field elevation to 2500 feet, selected flight level change (FLCH) and selected 290 in the heading window with HDG (Heading) selected. During the climb and turn, the Captain (PF) asked me to set the IAS speed to 190 from 180, at which time I advocated we stay at 180 IAS because my high speed awareness was showing the max speed of 195 for the flaps 20 limitation. Some confusion occurred as his speed tape was reflecting a high speed limit of 210 for the flaps 15 limit. I took notice of the difference and verbalized it. We eventually got the airspeed back to 180 but were briefly flying between 195 - 200 IAS as we contacted Departure Control. Once stable, Autopilot back ON and fully able to ascertain our course of action, we discussed flying & non-flying duties and [requested priority handling]. I remained as the pilot monitoring (PM) and initiated the non-normal checklist. Upon arriving at the deferred descent checklist" items, we attempted to contact ZZZ station operations. Multiple attempts (~3x) on XXX.XX and XXX.XXX each were made before finally making contact with ZZZ Maintenance (XXX.XXY). Our situation we relayed and asked to forward to station operations. The flight attendants were advised & given a briefing and a passenger announcement was made. At which time we reset the FMC for the ILS XXL, briefed, completed the deferred descent checklist items and turned back towards ZZZ for approach and landing. The approach and landing was as expected with the higher the normal approach speed. Upon clearing the runway, no further assistance was required from the Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) and we taxied to the gate. During taxi-in, the EICAS message cleared and both flap position indicators moved to the commanded flaps 20 position. Once at the gate and shutdown, we debriefed the event. Flap handle and FLAP GPWS override remained selected for Maintenance." While slowing and configuring for approach to land in ZZZ, recieved TE Flap Asym EICAS message while moving flaps from15 to 20. Performed normal go around while keeping flaps in current position, received delay vectors while [requesting priority handling] and completing required emergency procedures and notifications. Returned to ZZZ for ILS XXL, with flaps between 15 and 20 for uneventful landing and taxi to gate.
ASRSN:2241997.s: The flight crew experienced a TE FLAP ASYM EICAS message while extending flaps from 15 to 20 on approach to ZZZ, prompting a go-around and speed confusion due to conflicting high-speed limit indications. After contacting maintenance and completing checklists, they returned for an uneventful ILS landing with asymmetric flaps, which normalized during taxi-in.

ASRSN:2242062.n: I have seen this same situation numerous times on the 737, but not all the time. On the CAVLR6 STAR, there is a crossing restriction to cross PERKN at or above FL220. About 75% of the time on this arrival, we receive a 'steep descent after PERKN' message on the FMC, but this time we did not. Autopilot was ON, FO was flying pilot, LNAV and VNAV engaged, ATC gave a 'descend via the CAVLR6, landing south.' 4000 feet was set in the altitude window. We began the VNAV descent out of FL250, and when we got close to PERKN, although the autopilot was ON, and LNAV and VNAV were engaged, the autopilot did not abide by the altitude restriction of FL220 or above at PERKN. We were about two miles from PERKN descending through FL220, and since it happened so quick, it was quicker for me as the pilot monitoring (PM), to click off the autopilot and level the airplane to try and abide by the altitude restriction at PERKN. Before I could stop the airplane from descending, we had descended to approximately 21,700 about 1.5 miles prior to PERKN. I then handed the airplane back to the FO, and he continued to slowly climb us back to FL220. As always on this STAR, the profile is way too steep for the airplane directly after PERKN, so the VNAV PATH dropped into VNAV SPD, and we were high on the descent path. The FO reengaged the autopilot and used speed brakes to try and descend to get us on the VNAV PATH. We continued the descend via clearance, but barely made the altitude and speed restriction at CAVLR because the airplane had a steep descent after PERKN. The rest of the arrival was uneventful, and we continued to a landing.I normally see this situation when we have a very strong tailwind, but today we had a quartering headwind of approximately 25 kt.The descent profile for this STAR is way too steep for the 737 right after the PERKN intersection. For some reason, even though there is a big altitude restriction window at KHOOD, the software program of this airplane wants to start an extremely steep descent after PERKN, sometimes up to 4,000 - 6,000 FPM rate of descent.
ASRSN:2242062.s: During a 737 arrival on the CAVLR6 STAR, the autopilot failed to maintain the FL220 crossing restriction at PERKN despite VNAV engagement, causing a descent to 21,700 feet. The pilot monitoring manually leveled the aircraft, but the steep descent profile and lack of a "steep descent" FMC message resulted in a marginal arrival at the CAVLR restriction.

ASRSN:2242121.n: As we were taxing to Runway XXR we stopped short of the runway, number 3 for take off. We started to smell and comment to each other about a gas like smell. Just then Tower notified us that the aircraft behind us noticed a fluid leaking out of the #1 engine. With the fumes we ran the quick action items for fumes and that started to help with fumes. And then shut the #1 engine down. Shortly after that we were made aware that ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) had been dispatched. We worked our way through the QRH for a fuel leak. The Captain ran coms between Maintenance, Dispatch, and ZZZ Opps. ARFF determined that it was fuel leaking but had stopped leaking after we shut the #1 down. With the leak stopped and ARFF behind us we determined it was safe to taxi back to the gate. Once at the gate we deplaned the aircraft and handed the keys to ZZZ Maintenance Cause: Luckily we were stopped and had the parking brake set. Team work and task management helped get through the required tasks. Conformation between pilots that we were safe and making good discussions moving forward do not add more issues to the situation.
ASRSN:2242121.s: Pilots detected a fuel leak from the #1 engine while taxiing to Runway XXR, prompting an engine shutdown and ARFF dispatch. The leak stopped after shutdown, allowing the crew to safely taxi back to the gate and deplane passengers.

ASRSN:2242127.n: Known GPS jamming/spoofing. Unreliable GPS readings, ADS-B, ATC transponder fail lights illuminated. Position accuracy slightly degraded.Cause: Used land based navigation aids to verify aircraft position during the outage which lasted approximately 40 minutes. Notified ATC, and Dispatch. Position and aircraft navigation were not affected. All systems recovered except GPS 2, which recovered on the ground in ONT after realigning at the gate.
ASRSN:2242127.s: The crew experienced GPS jamming causing unreliable readings and transponder failures for 40 minutes. They verified position using land-based aids, notified ATC and Dispatch, and recovered all systems except GPS 2, which realigned on the ground at ONT.

ASRSN:2242128.n: After changing runways due to crosswinds at/exceeding CAT 2 limits, we used the 13L CAT 2. The clearance was direct KMCHI, cross BUZON at 2900 cleared ILS 13L. The intercept of the localizer is so close in that we completely missed the glideslope and missed the approach. On second attempt we studied the problem closer and VNAV'd to 1500 to capture the glideslope and all went fine. This approach is a bit odd and could use some kind of warning language to alert crews of the difficulty capturing the glideslope very close in and at a low altitude. We missed and the flight behind us missed, I am betting ATC is wondering why the high number of missed approaches? I spoke to a friend at a different airline to ask if this was a common problem, he said they are not authorized by their company to use that approach. I feel that we need to investigate this issue and warn crews about this unique approach.Cause: Unusual approach, that is doable but could use some 'heads up' notation about glideslope intercept at low altitude and close in, or something helpful.
ASRSN:2242128.s: The crew missed the ILS 13L approach twice due to a difficult glideslope intercept at low altitude and close range after a direct clearance to KMCHI. The reporter attributes the issue to the unusual approach design and recommends adding warning language to alert crews.

ASRSN:2242136.n: After the end of boarding, the red ECAM SMOKE AFT CARGO SMOKE illuminated along with the master warning red light. Because we were at the gate with the cargo doors open this is a procedure where we need to go to the ramp to verify. FO went down to the ramp while CA called the aft FA (Flight Attendant) station and asked them to asses their environment. Once we determined it to be an actual event, we directed the FA crew to do the Emergency Deplane procedure. As pax (Passengers) and crew were deplaning, the crew reported seeing a light haze in the air. Much later, we learned from maintenance they believed the fire bottle squib fired in an electrical malfunction releasing the retardant into the empty aft cargo compartment.Cause: Unknown cause, maintenance believes a possible electrical malfunction in the cargo fire supression squib.
ASRSN:2242136.s: The flight crew received a false aft cargo smoke warning at the gate with open doors, triggering an emergency deplaning. Maintenance later attributed the event to an electrical malfunction that inadvertently fired the fire suppression squib into the empty compartment.

ASRSN:2242139.n: GPS jamming incident. Additional information. Upon reading the reports necessary I found that a maintenance logbook entry was required which I didn't create thinking this was the signal issue not an aircraft issue.Cause: Unfamiliar with this issue. Approximately 1 hour into cruise flight, we received an ECAM NAV FM/GPS POS DISAGREE. GPS 2 went offline. We notified ATC and was advised that it would return approximately 80 miles from the destination. It would intermittently return with a downgraded notification. While on descent, the GPS went offline again. Since TUS requires an approach to be flown at night, we chose to fly the VOR 30. The approach was armed but the final approach course never captured. The approach was hand-flown/raw data. Other planes on the frequency were experiencing the same issue. Requires investigation.
ASRSN:2242139.s: The crew experienced GPS jamming during cruise and descent, causing NAV FM/GPS POS DISAGREE and loss of GPS 2. Due to unfamiliarity with the issue, no maintenance logbook entry was created, and the crew hand-flew a VOR 30 approach after the final course failed to capture.

ASRSN:2242143.n: Approximately 50 miles west of CIKAN GPS 2 started to falter and lose integrity dropping offline. Went to QRH and completed procedure which was the message presented on ECAM. We reached out to Dispatch to inform them of situation and their response was to also run [another] procedure, which we did and completed this as well. While completing the QRH procedures we advised ATC of the situation. When advised of this we were told, Yeah expect that until almost TUS." We continued to actively monitor FMGC integrity and position to maintain accurate navigation. When handed off to TUS we advised them of the situation as well and they advised it should come back as we get closer. We continued to monitor the GPS and saw that GPS 1 was coming back, it managed to obtain 10 satellite signals before quickly dropping back down and losing integrity again. It never recovered a signal strong enough to become reliable. At this point we requested to VOR 30 which we were vectored for as we had briefed previously as a backup in case of the GPS not coming back. After being cleared for the approach it was armed and did not acquire the approach accurately to which we then continued the approach hand-flown / raw data. The box had become what we think was lost and contributed to this issue of the approach. Cause: GPS jamming that was not NOTAM'd out in the area."
ASRSN:2242143.s: The flight crew experienced GPS 2 failure and subsequent GPS 1 signal loss due to unreported jamming while approaching TUS. After failing to acquire the VOR 30 approach automatically, they completed a hand-flown raw data approach.

ASRSN:2242148.n: About 45 after departure, level at FL370 the parking brake light illuminated. Conferred with Dispatch and Maintenance via crew phone. Determined light received signal and current from a brake SOV (Shut Off Valve) as well as a parking brake set" relay. This confirmed to me the possibility of engaged parking brake at landing. No checklist in QRH. Used "tire failure" information and pilot reasoning for discussion. Crew discussed tire failure, brake fire, and complete loss of aircraft control. No immediate safety of flight existed. About 3 hours remaining in flight. Weather in ZZZ suitable. Developed contingency of ZZZ1 if weather degraded (temp and due point spread 2 degrees). Relayed, to dispatch, intention to [request priority handling] with ZZZ center in a few hours. Continued to destination. 1:20 prior to landing, coordinated necessary preparation time with #1 FA (Flight Attendant). Performed all call and gave briefing. Roughly XA:25. Elected to defer PAX (Passenger) PA to XB:00, 45 prior to landing. Made PA and FAs completed pre evacuation duties, moving passengers away from wings (brake fire location) towards door exits. Upon initial contact with ZZZ center, [requested priority handling], requested ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) and runway XXC with long final and early descent to 5000'. Transferred aircraft to CA for landing. Depressurized cabin per procedure at 5000' and FO made "Brace" at 250' AGL. On landing no abnormalities were observed. ARFF confirmed brake temps and tire conditions normal. Light was illuminated on touchdown and rollout. After setting of parking brake for passenger PA, light extinguished on next parking brake release. Taxied to gate uneventful. The entire cabin crew deserves high marks for professionalism and being a useful and helpful part of the process. They used their own creative reasoning (given the precise mechanical situation) but conferred with the Captain to complete the communication circle. I know it was unusual and stressful at times. It was burden-lifting to be able to give the briefing and have confidence the passengers were prepared for the grave possibilities at landing. The cabin department should know of a job well done for training preparedness and leadership shown by my crew. Cause: Mechanical failure. Risks were mitigated with quick, frank, accurate and respectful communication via ACARS and Crew Phone with Dispatch and Maintenance. Commendable professionalism from cabin crew and first officer as well!"
ASRSN:2242148.s: The flight crew managed a false parking brake light indication at FL370 caused by a mechanical failure, coordinating with maintenance and requesting priority handling and ARFF. The aircraft landed safely with no abnormalities, and the cabin crew effectively prepared passengers for potential evacuation.

ASRSN:2242176.n: Operating Aircraft X ZZZ1-ZZZ. Weather was VMC. We were given vectors for RNAV XXR and subsequently cleared for approach from ZZZZZ fix (10.4 from runway). We maintained assigned altitude until we were on approach as cleared by Approach Control. Once established we met all altitudes per charted procedures. We checked on with Tower and was told to report final approach fix ZZZZZ1 (3.9 from runway). Charted altitude for ZZZZZ1 is 2,300. We were at altitude and fully configured. As we approached ZZZZZ1 tower gave us location of traffic that was to the west of us and above our altitude. Traffic was a T-38 military training aircraft. We did not have visual on them but the TCAS was showing them to the west. Last altitude I noticed on TCAS was 4,000 ft. A few seconds later we received an RA with descend guidance. We were at ZZZZZ1. The military trainer flew directly overhead, at 2,500, same fix on the same course for XXR. My estimation was 200 feet vertical separation. We followed RA and then initiated a GO-AROUND once we could see we were clear of traffic. Estimated speed of T-38 was 300 knots. We were given vectors back around and approach and landing was uneventful.The major issue with ZZZ is military aircraft and civilian aircraft are not talking/listening on same frequencies. Military is using UHF and more than likely are not equipped with TCAS. Additionally, most of the military aircraft are students in high speed jets and many are foreign military personnel as well. This is a huge safety concern. Mitigation could be same frequencies. Additionally, maybe using one runway for civilian aircraft instead of sharing the same runways and approaches with high speed and saturated military aircraft. This was an extremely close call.Military and civilian aircraft need to be on same frequency. Military aircraft should be equipped and operating TCAS systems if they are operating in same location as civilian aircraft. This is too similar to the company X accident. This was so close and completely avoidable. Estimation was 200 feet vertical separation.
ASRSN:2242176.s: Pilots of Aircraft X ZZZ1-ZZZ received a TCAS descent RA at the ZZZZZ1 fix while a T-38 military trainer flew overhead at 2,500 feet, resulting in an estimated 200-foot vertical separation. The crew executed a go-around, attributing the conflict to military and civilian aircraft operating on different frequencies without TCAS coordination.

ASRSN:2242203.n: During approach into ZZZ, an EMB-145 that landed prior to us suffered some sort of hydraulic failure that left them unable to exit the runway. This prompted ATC to direct us to go around. At this point, we had approximately 3400 pounds of fuel onboard.We had no alternate, as the weather was VFR. I asked ATC how long they thought it would take to get a tug out to the disabled aircraft and they told us it would be at least half an hour, maybe more, but no guarantees. They also told us that if we needed to land on the closed runway, we could, however there would be no place for us to deplane our passengers, or even make it to a gate due to the taxiway construction.I immediately started looking for nearby airports within our fuel range and made the decision to divert to ZZZ1. At the time I requested to divert, we had approximately 3200 pounds of fuel. The distance that I calculated was approximately 114 nautical miles. I figured we would burn about 1200 pounds of fuel based on an average fuel burn of 100 pounds per 10 nautical miles. I elected to climb to 10,000 feet for better fuel economy based on my experience from flying shorter flights out of ZZZ2.I sent an ACARS to dispatch that we were diverting to ZZZ1 and they got back to me promptly with an amended release. I sent our distance from ZZZ1 with our fuel on board and new altitude. Dispatch sent back a message that had our burn off going into our reserve fuel. I declared minimum fuel with approach. Once we leveled off at 10,000 feet, I had the First Officer reduce the fuel flow to 1000 pph per side. We had approximately 2800 pounds of fuel and were about 25 minutes out. I calculated that we would land with about 1800 pounds of fuel. Our reserve fuel was 1641 pounds.I then notified the flight attendant of the diversion for the disabled aircraft and made an announcement to the passengers to let them know what was going on and that we would be landing soon and I would have more information on the ground.The First Officer did an excellent job of preparing the aircraft for approach into ZZZ1. He had set up for the approach and prepared his briefing while I was task saturated.As we got closer to ZZZ1 and began our flight idle descent, I declared emergency fuel. Our fuel burn was not indicating that we would land below our reserve of 1641 pounds but it was close enough that any deviation would put us there. We landed safely on runway XXR in ZZZ1 with 2000 pounds of fuel on board.Suggestion: Try to plan ahead for situations that could occur with only one runway available. We were lucky to be tankering on this flight to even have enough fuel to divert to a different airport. I'm glad we did end up diverting because that disabled aircraft didn't get off the runway until we had been parked for about 20 minutes in ZZZ1.
ASRSN:2242203.s: The crew of an EMB-145 diverted to ZZZ1 after a preceding aircraft's hydraulic failure blocked the runway at ZZZ, forcing a go-around. Declaring minimum and emergency fuel due to the delay, they landed safely at ZZZ1 with 2,000 pounds remaining.

ASRSN:2242231.n: My first officer and I were cleared for takeoff from runway XXR we were still in the process of aligning with the centerline and had not advanced the throttles with intent to depart when my First Officer and I assessed that the spacing with the aircraft on short final for Runway XYR appeared tighter than ideal. In the interest of safety and to avoid any potential conflict, we made the decision to hold momentarily and allow the inbound aircraft to pass. Approximately 30 seconds after the initial clearance, we were re-cleared for takeoff and proceeded with the remainder of the flight without issue.Out of respect for the controller's judgment and to maintain a good rapport, we chose our wording carefully to avoid any unnecessary scrutiny or misinterpretation. This may have lead to a misunderstanding as to the reason why we denied the takeoff clearance.
ASRSN:2242231.s: The pilot and first officer held on Runway XXR after takeoff clearance due to tight spacing with an aircraft on short final for Runway XYR. They proceeded after a 30-second delay, though their careful wording to the controller may have caused a misunderstanding regarding the reason for the hold.

ASRSN:2242292.n: Night VFR flight with commercial student pilot from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. We noticed low oil pressure approximately 70 miles west of ZZZ2. Oil annunciator light was flickering, and that was when we saw oil pressure was in the yellow arc. We went through troubleshooting the issue with reference to the POH, and alerted ATC of the problem. The oil annunciator light then went from flickering to a steady glow, which then my student and I decided to [advise ATC]. We [advised ATC on] XXX.XX ZZZ center. We then corrected to divert to ZZZ3 and overfly the road in the event that we had total engine failure we would have a set place to land. We were informed by ZZZ Center that ZZZ3's runway was closed per NOTAM and ZZZ4 was the next closest option. The oil pressure had steadily continued to decrease since our first indication, at this point we made the decision to [request priority handling] to ZZZ Center. We were handed off to ZZZ approach where we were given a bravo clearance after requesting to remain at 9500 feet until ZZZ4. Upon reaching ZZZ4 we circled down and had an uneventful landing. The oil pressure had little to no reading at the time of landing.
ASRSN:2242292.s: A commercial student pilot and instructor experienced decreasing oil pressure and a steady annunciator light during a night VFR flight. They diverted to ZZZ4 after ZZZ3 was closed, received priority handling, and landed safely with negligible oil pressure.

ASRSN:2242298.n: A student and myself were flying back into ZZZ from the north practice area in a Cessna Skyhawk at 6500' MSL southbound. We were on frequency with ZZZ Tower inbound for a full stop. From ZZZ1 was another plane performing circles at 6500' just north of the ZZZ delta airspace. Not on radio contact with them on XXX.XXX practice frequency prior to switching to XXX.X. ZZZ Tower gave a traffic advisory to us regarding their position only after we had taken evasive action. I misunderstood Tower controller's instruction to switch from right downwind for Rwy XXR to base for XXL following a Cessna. I had been following a Bonanza on right downwind. I turned right base for XXL too early and had to maneuver to avoid an aircraft on final for XXR.
ASRSN:2242298.s: A student and pilot in a Cessna Skyhawk at 6,500 feet southbound near ZZZ took evasive action after misinterpreting a Tower instruction to switch from right downwind to base. This error caused an early turn that required maneuvering to avoid an aircraft on final for Runway XXR.
